title: Best value per kilo, best bag?
hook: Pack the best value per kilo first. Is that the most value a 50 kg bag can hold?

doesNotKnow: that best value per kilo first fails when items cannot be cut, and works when they can

misconception: Packing the best value-for-weight items first always fills a bag best.
objective: The learner can explain that best-value-per-kilo-first is best when items can be cut, but with whole items it leaves a gap that only a different combination fills.

claims.text: The 10 kg item is worth $6 per kg, the 20 kg item $5 per kg and the 30 kg item $4 per kg.
claims.source: 60 / 10 = 6, 100 / 20 = 5, 120 / 30 = 4 (builder, node). Printed on each shelf item in Demo.tsx.

claims.text: Best value per kilo first with whole items packs the 10 kg and 20 kg items for $160, leaving 20 kg empty, and the 30 kg item no longer fits.
claims.source: Builder's node script (company/reviews/knapsack-ratio-trap/verify.mjs): items sorted by value per kg, added while they fit: 10 kg, 20 kg, then 30 kg > 20 kg free. Total $160, 20 kg free. Stage starts in this state.

claims.text: With whole items, the best bag that fits 50 kg is the 20 kg and 30 kg items for $220.
claims.source: Builder's node script over all 8 subsets of the 3 items: fitting subsets are {} 0, {10} 60, {20} 100, {10,20} 160, {30} 120, {10,30} 180, {20,30} 220 (50 kg); {10,20,30} is 60 kg and does not fit. Maximum $220.

claims.text: When items can be cut, best value per kilo first packs the 10 kg item, the 20 kg item and two thirds of the 30 kg item for $240.
claims.source: Builder's node script: greedy by ratio taking min(weight, room) of each: 10 kg ($60) + 20 kg ($100) + 20 of 30 kg ($80) = $240 (20 / 30 = two thirds). Stage's cut bag starts in this state.

claims.text: When items can be cut, no bag does better than best value per kilo first.
claims.source: Fractional knapsack: greedy by value per kilo is optimal (Cormen, Leiserson, Rivest, Stein, Introduction to Algorithms; section 16.2 in the 3rd edition, with this 10 / 20 / 30 kg, $60 / $100 / $120 example in its Figure 16.2). Section number in the 4th edition (content/works.json clrs-4e) not checked by the builder. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: verified by derivation (exchange argument: any optimal fractional bag can swap weight toward a higher value-per-kg item without losing value) and own node grid search over fractional amounts (max $240). CLRS 3e numbering (§16.2, Fig. 16.2, Ex. 16.2-1) confirmed against exercise indexes; in 4e greedy is Chapter 15 (TOC confirmed), section number not opened, so cite 4e as ch. 15 or confirm §15.2 before using it.

claims.text: Dynamic programming finds the best whole-item bag without trying every combination.
claims.source: 0/1 knapsack in O(nW) time by dynamic programming (CLRS 3rd edition exercise 16.2-2), against 2^n subsets by trying all of them. Told in the reveal, not shown. · Fact-check pass 19 2026-10-14: verified by own 0/1 DP (n x W table, 93 cell updates for n = 3, W = 50, gives $220) against 2^3 = 8 subsets. CLRS 3e Ex. 16.2-2 (O(nW) DP) confirmed against exercise indexes; 4e number not opened.

recall.question: A bag holds 10 kg. Items: 6 kg worth $60, 5 kg worth $45, 5 kg worth $45. Whole items only. Best value per kilo first takes the 6 kg item. Is that the best bag?
options: Yes, it has the best value per kilo
No, the two 5 kg items fill it for $90
recall.why: The 6 kg item is $10 per kg, so it goes first, but then 4 kg is left and neither 5 kg item fits: $60. The two 5 kg items fill the bag exactly for $90. All three would weigh 16 kg.

references.note: Greedy strategy; 0-1 vs fractional knapsack (3rd ed. 16.2, Figure 16.2); section number in 4th edition unchecked
